facts.name: Harebell
facts.light: Full sun for the most flowers; takes part shade
facts.moisture: Dry to average; sandy or rocky soil is fine
facts.notes: Dainty blue bells nodding on thread-thin stems from early summer into fall. Tougher than it looks: it grows on Michigan's sand dunes and in rock cracks, and handles drought. Plant it in a group near the front of the bed, where taller plants won't crowd it out. Not the weedy creeping bellflower, which has bigger flowers and wider leaves.

sources.note: Michigan Wild Ones plant sheet: harebells grow in clumps on many Michigan dunes; 6 to 18 in; blooms early summer into late fall.

sources.title: Wild Cherry Farm (Michigan native nursery): Harebell
sources.note: Sold as a native plant by a Michigan nursery; 12 in, blooms June to September, full to part sun, dry soil, deer resistant.

sources.title: New Moon Nurseries: Campanula rotundifolia
sources.note: Drought tolerant; 6 to 18 in tall, about 1 ft wide; zones 3 to 8.

sources.title: Wild Ones River City Chapter (Grand Rapids): Harebell
sources.note: Full sun gives the most flowers; dry to average soil. Thin out taller, aggressive neighbors that crowd it. Young plants may flop for a couple of years and do best in groups. Seedlings bloom in their second year.

companions.why: Good companions: pussytoes, nodding wild onion, columbine, prairie smoke and beardtongues.
